The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: computing and data foundations, problem decomposition and modeling, engineering implementation and verification, and written and oral expression. The real difference lies in the objective and responsibility: the management direction aims at coordinating people and budget and projects; the systems analysis direction aims at transforming requirements into solutions and delivering them; the database architecture direction aims at data models and storage governance; the data science direction aims at data-driven modeling and business delivery; while this occupation centers on basic research and the study and verification of new principles and new technology, with papers and methods and reproducible results as its main output. Use CS-17 in section 09 to compare the supplied benchmark records and draft a question for the research lead. Use W-CS to check the metric version and workload, then keep unresolved evidence open. No experiment, code or real dataset is needed.

The comparison basis is the occupational definition and tasks and work activities and work context descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 15-1221.00 page, the related occupations and adjacent occupation codes listed on that page, the adjacent occupation slug list registered in this evidence route, and the public occupational materials for each adjacent occupation; the comparison is an editorial compilation and does not constitute ethical, legal, intellectual property or research evaluation conclusions.

The table below compares the positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: computer and information systems managers, architectural and engineering managers, natural sciences managers, computer systems analysts, database architects and data scientists. The four columns each answer the same kind of question: what the direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choosing it.

Computer and information systems managers coordinate the people, budget, projects and compliance of the information technology department, aimed at the stable operation and delivery of business systems; this occupation centers on basic research and the creation and verification of new principles and new technology.
People willing to coordinate the IT department and project delivery suit that direction; people willing to do basic research and verify new methods suit this occupation.
Mainly department management and enterprise system delivery and operations records.
Computer and information systems managers

Architectural and engineering managers coordinate the schedule, budget, people and compliance of engineering projects; this occupation mainly produces research problems and methods in the computer and information field.
People willing to coordinate engineering projects and teams suit that direction; people willing to do theory and method research suit this occupation.
Mainly engineering project management and acceptance records.
Architectural and engineering managers

Natural sciences managers coordinate natural science teams and projects and their compliance; this occupation's research object is the principles and systems of computing and information, not natural science phenomena themselves.
People willing to coordinate natural science teams and projects suit that direction; people willing to study computing and information principles suit this occupation.
Mainly natural science project management and experimental platform records.
Natural sciences managers

Computer systems analysts mainly translate business requirements into system solutions and coordinate implementation; this occupation mainly proposes and verifies new theories or methods and technical solutions, and does not carry responsibility for business system delivery.
People willing to do requirements analysis and system solution coordination suit that direction; people willing to do principle and method innovation suit this occupation.
Mainly requirements and solutions and implementation coordination records.
Computer systems analysts

Database architects mainly design and govern databases and data models and storage solutions; this occupation addresses broader computer and information science research problems and may involve hardware and algorithms and systems.
People willing to do data model and storage and governance design suit that direction; people willing to do principle and method research suit this occupation.
Mainly data model and database design and governance records.
Database architects

Data scientists mainly deliver data-driven modeling and analysis, aimed at business or product conclusions; this occupation focuses more on the novelty and reproducibility of the method itself and may extend to hardware and systems and theory.
People willing to deliver business conclusions through data modeling suit that direction; people willing to study new methods and new principles suit this occupation.
Mainly data modeling and analysis methods and business delivery records.
Data scientists

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires filling in new competencies and qualifications: the department management direction requires people and budget and compliance management experience; the engineering project management direction requires engineering schedule and acceptance management experience; the natural sciences management direction requires project coordination experience in the natural sciences; the systems analysis direction requires requirements analysis and business modeling and implementation coordination experience; the database architecture direction requires engineering experience in data models and storage and governance; the data science direction requires data modeling and business delivery experience. Computing and modeling and verification abilities can transfer, but the objectives and responsibility boundaries of each direction must be rebuilt.

entries: Fit signal: you are willing to write the problem to a testable degree and define the evaluation metrics and baseline in advance.
Fit signal: when a flaw in the method or reproduction is pointed out, you go back to the experiment and code to verify rather than defending yourself first.

paragraphs: The current O*NET list has 33 knowledge items, 52 ability items and 21 work styles; inquisitiveness 100 / innovation 94 / attention to detail 83 / adaptability 77 / achievement 75, knowledge computers 89 / mathematics 77 / engineering 74 / English 72, abilities deductive and inductive 78 / oral comprehension and expression 75 / problem sensitivity and written comprehension 72. entries: Fit signal: you habitually record the environment and dependencies and randomness and data versions and results so that others can reproduce them.
Editorial self-check: sitting posture, working hours, deadlines and collaboration conditions are verified by target position, and O*NET respondent distributions are not the form of every position.

paragraphs: Caution: adjusting metrics or selectively presenting experiments to obtain "better-looking" results directly amplifies risk in peer review, reproduction and academic integrity.

Interest orientation: the occupation page's interest code is IC (Investigative, Conventional), and the daily tasks are mainly problem definition and theoretical modeling, system and tool implementation and experimentation, and team and research organization and output.

entries: Fit signal: if you enjoy narrowing a vague problem to a verifiable form, you can try it and observe whether you feel a sense of achievement.
Fit signal: if you are more focused on systems and engineering implementation, the system and tool implementation and experimentation direction can likewise be developed over the long term.
Fit signal: willingness to verify your own suitability by "doing one method and experiment plan and asking someone to review it" rather than "saying you have written a lot of code."
Fit signal: you can take the initiative to correct after a missing item in the method or records is pointed out and form a habit of verification.

paragraphs: Caution: Enneagram interpretations easily slide into personality diagnosis, and this page does not use it to judge fit.

This occupation has a clear substantive requirement for computing and mathematics and engineering knowledge: the O*NET knowledge list is led by computers and electronics 89, mathematics 77, engineering and technology 74, English language 72, administration and management 58, design 57; the ability list is led by deductive reasoning and inductive reasoning (both 78), oral comprehension and expression (both 75), fluency of ideas and problem sensitivity and written comprehension (all 72); the skills list is led by critical thinking 75, active listening and reading comprehension (both 69), active learning and oral expression (both 63), mathematics and writing (both 60).

entries: Fit signal: you can compare theoretical derivations with experimental results to judge whether the conclusion holds up.
Fit signal: you are willing to use version control and experiment management tools for repetitive work, leaving your attention for the problem and method.

paragraphs: Caution: relying on personal memory over the long term without recording the environment and dependencies and data and results will expose risk during reproduction, review and team handover; fixing the process and the documentation is the sustainable approach.

Communication context: email 100% every day, face-to-face 69% every day and 31% at least once a week but not every day, telephone 64% every day; 51% consider teamwork extremely important and 43% very important; external communication 49% extremely important and 33% fairly important, coordination 25% extremely important and 27% very important. Respondent distributions are not a requirement for all positions or a personal ability standard.

entries: Fit signal: you can diagnose "an experiment that does not support the hypothesis" separately from "a problem with the method," and rule them out item by item from the records.
